## The puzzle

```{=html}
<div class="concise-only">
```

On 8 April 2026, Pakistan brokered a US-Iran ceasefire. Nine days later, the first violations: Iran attempted Hormuz transits; the US did not reciprocally lift any sanctions. On 20 April, the US Navy seized the tanker *Touska*. On 4 May, Operation Project Freedom sank six IRGCN fast attack craft. On 7-8 May, US strikes on Bandar Abbas and Qeshm; UAE shootdowns; US strikes on empty oil tankers. One month from signing, the ceasefire is in operational collapse. Why?

```{=html}
</div>
<div class="deep-only">
```

On 8 April 2026, after six weeks of war following the 28 February strikes, Pakistan brokered a US-Iran ceasefire agreement. Nine days later — on 17-18 April — the first violations registered: Iran attempted a Hormuz transit against the agreement's no-transit understanding; the US did not reciprocally lift any sanctions as the agreement contemplated. On 20 April the US Navy seized the tanker *Touska* in a denial-coded operation that signaled the ceasefire's enforcement provisions were not binding US action. On 4 May Operation Project Freedom (the US-led Hormuz reopening) sank six IRGCN fast attack craft in escort operations. On 7 May US strikes hit IRGCN command nodes at Bandar Abbas and Qeshm. On 8 May UAE Patriot batteries shot down inbound missiles; US strikes destroyed two empty oil tankers off the Iranian coast in what analysts read as denial signaling. One month from signing, the ceasefire is in operational collapse, the dual blockade continues, and the war is back to active hostilities. Why? The standard "ceasefires fail because the underlying disputes are unresolved" answer is too thin — it doesn't explain the specific 9-days-later trajectory, doesn't engage why Pakistan failed where some mediators succeed, and cannot distinguish between the ceasefire being unstable and the war being stable. The puzzle Q3 sets: *what specifically — mechanism by mechanism — broke the Pakistan-brokered ceasefire so quickly?*

## Methodology — Tier-2 abbreviated protocol + the project's most aggressive mechanism reduction

This chapter applies the Tier-2 abbreviated protocol with three new corpus acquisitions (Beardsley 2008 primary, Werner-Yuen 2005 primary, Greig 2005 compilation). The candidate mechanism set reduced from *seventeen* to three via META rule 4 discipline — the most aggressive reduction in any Q-execution so far, justified because the corpus is unusually rich for Q3 and many mechanisms converge on the same outcome through related theoretical pathways. The reduced three (α' + β' + γ') have natively distinct literature domains: mediation-specific (Beardsley + Werner-Yuen), structural-commitment-trap (Walter + Werner 1999 + Powell-Reiter + Pape + Schelling), and spoiler/mediator/two-level-actor (Stedman + Kydd + Putnam). Q3 is the fifth principled-multi-framework case in the project; the pattern is well-validated. The headline posterior at 0.75 is the highest in the Tier-2 cluster (vs Q10 at 0.55; Q2 at 0.65) due to strong empirical T1 foundation (the violation cascade is directly observable) and strong T2 framework foundation (Beardsley + Werner-Yuen empirics directly apply).

::: {focus-on="cr-stage1"}
[**The violation cascade.** Nine days after the 8 April signing, the first violations — Iran's Hormuz transit attempt and the US's failure to reciprocally lift sanctions — registered. Twelve days later, the *Touska* seizure. By 4 May, active escort combat. By 7-8 May, expanded strikes. One month from signing, the ceasefire is in operational collapse. This is the **textbook Beardsley + Werner-Yuen failure pattern** — the operational time-inconsistency trajectory in real time.]{.concise-only}

::: {.deep-only}
**The 8 April → 8 May violation cascade.** Pakistan brokered the 8 April 2026 ceasefire after six weeks of active war following the 28 February strikes. The agreement contemplated a phased no-transit / sanctions-lift exchange with monitoring promises. *17-18 April — first violations*: Iran attempted a Hormuz transit against the agreement's no-transit understanding (a contested test of US restraint); the US did not reciprocally lift any sanctions as the agreement's first phase contemplated. This is the [Beardsley time-inconsistency]{.gloss data-gloss="beardsley-mediation-time-inconsistency"} mechanism in execution: the agreement's terms required reciprocal performance neither side was structurally willing to deliver without external compulsion. *20 April — *Touska* seizure*: the US Navy seized the tanker *Touska* in a denial-coded operation that signaled enforcement-side hardening. *4 May — Operation Project Freedom launches*: the US-led Hormuz reopening sank six IRGCN fast attack craft in escort operations; this is a fundamental violation of the ceasefire's no-active-hostilities provision. *7 May — strikes on Bandar Abbas and Qeshm*: US strikes hit IRGCN command nodes inside Iranian territory; ceasefire is now in active collapse. *8 May — multi-axis escalation*: UAE Patriot batteries shot down inbound missiles; US strikes destroyed two empty oil tankers off the Iranian coast in denial signaling. *The trajectory matches Beardsley + Werner-Yuen predictions point-by-point*: mediator-induced agreement (Pakistan pressure), short-term success (formal signing), rapid time-inconsistency manifestation (9-day onset of violations), accelerating cascade through 30 days as battle-inconsistency + interrupted-war pattern asserted themselves.
:::

::: {focus-on="cr-stage2"}
[**α' — [Beardsley mediation-time-inconsistency]{.gloss data-gloss="beardsley-mediation-time-inconsistency"} + [Werner-Yuen H1+H2]{.gloss data-gloss="werner-yuen-ceasefire-failure"}**. Mediator pressure artificially expanded the apparent bargaining range; once Pakistan's leverage decayed, the range contracted and the agreement fell outside it. H1 (battle-inconsistency) and H2 (interrupted-war) both fire. Historical cases firing both — Korean 1953, Indo-Pakistani 1948/65/71, Israel-Egypt 1948-67-73, Minsk I/II — all failed at very high rate.]{.concise-only}

::: {.deep-only}
**Mechanism α' — [Beardsley mediation-induced time-inconsistency]{.gloss data-gloss="beardsley-mediation-time-inconsistency"} under interrupted-war + battle-inconsistency** (P operative 0.95; P load-bearing 0.65). The framework combination: Beardsley 2008 established empirically across the 1918-2001 international-crisis-behavior dataset that mediated crises fail at higher long-term rate than unmediated ones — the mediator's artificial incentives (information provision, leveraging costs, monitoring/enforcement promises) temporarily expand the apparent bargaining range; once mediator influence wanes, the artificial expansion contracts. Werner-Yuen 2005 tested two hypotheses on 48 interstate wars 1946-1997: H1 — ceasefires after wars with *consistent battle outcomes* (both sides updated to revealed military reality) are at decreased risk of failure; H2 — ceasefires after *interrupted wars* (third-party pressure before military convergence) are at *increased* risk because terms don't reflect underlying balance of power. The Pakistan-brokered 2026 ceasefire fires both H1 and H2 simultaneously. *H1 (battle-inconsistency)*: Iran absorbed direct strikes on nuclear infrastructure, command nodes, and the Supreme Leader's location but retained chokepoint denial capacity, alternative architecture (renminbi-toll), and IRGC institutional consolidation. The US imposed massive costs but did not achieve denial of Iran's strategic options. Both sides retained reason to believe renewed war could yield better terms. *H2 (interrupted-war pattern)*: Pakistan's third-party pressure produced agreement before military convergence — neither side had yet reached the position where renewed fighting was clearly unprofitable. Historical cases firing both H1 and H2: Korean 1953 armistice (high-intensity stalemate; UN/US pressure; held as frozen conflict with persistent DMZ violations); Indo-Pakistani 1948 / 1965 / 1971 (UN-pressured; repeated failure); Israel-Egypt 1948-67-73 (UN/US-pressured; repeated failure until Camp David); Russia-Ukraine 2014-22 Minsk I/II (multilateral pressure; both failed within months). The 2026 Iran-US case is in this base-rate pattern. The 9-days-later first violations and 30-day cascade are *consistent with very-high-failure-rate base rate*. Counter-example: Iran-Iraq 1988 UN Resolution 598 held because both sides were financially/militarily exhausted — reservation points converged through exhaustion. This exception does not apply to 2026: neither side is exhausted; both retain substantial military capacity.
:::
:::

::: {focus-on="cr-stage3"}
[**β' — Structural infeasibility.** [Walter 1997]{.gloss data-gloss="walter-third-party-enforcement"} no third-party enforcer (Pakistan + Oman + China lack capacity + impartiality; UNSC vetoed). [Werner 1999]{.gloss data-gloss="werner-peace-durability"} all three diagnostics fail: issues unresolved (Iran's 14-point vs US terms — no overlap); enforcement absent (Walter unmet); balance-of-power inconsistent (Iran's revealed strategic options exceed settlement-acceptable terms). Structurally-locked-in.]{.concise-only}

::: {.deep-only}
**Mechanism β' — Structural infeasibility: no third-party enforcement + all three Werner diagnostics fail** (P operative 0.95; P load-bearing 0.60). The framework combination: [Walter 1997]{.gloss data-gloss="walter-third-party-enforcement"} argued civil-war and analogous interstate-war settlements require third-party security guarantee for credible commitment; without external enforcement, combatants cannot credibly disarm or comply because each fears the other will renege. [Werner 1999]{.gloss data-gloss="werner-peace-durability"} identified three jointly-necessary conditions for post-war peace durability: issue resolution, enforcement, balance-of-power consistency. The Q3 application: all three Werner diagnostics fail simultaneously. *Issue resolution*: Iran's 14-point framework (regime preservation, enrichment access, Hormuz-toll regime, sanctions relief, missile programs preserved, IAEA access limited) has no overlap with US terms (regime change or constrained Iranian regime, zero enrichment, free Hormuz transit, sanctions architecture preserved, missile programs dismantled, full IAEA access). The bargaining ranges are operationally empty per Q5. *Enforcement*: Pakistan lacks military capacity to compel either side; Oman is too small; China + Russia vetoed UNSC enforcement; US would veto Russia/China-led enforcement; no major-power coalition with both capacity and impartiality is available. *Balance-of-power consistency*: Iran's revealed strategic options (chokepoint denial, alternative architecture, renminbi-toll, IRGC consolidation) demonstrate continued bargaining power exceeding settlement-acceptable terms; any settlement would require Iran to accept terms premised on a post-strike weakened position that doesn't match revealed strength. Per META rule 3, β' is *structurally-locked-in for the war's foreseeable duration under current geopolitics*; no third-party-enforcer mechanism is on the horizon; Werner diagnostics will continue to fail.
:::
:::

::: {focus-on="cr-stage4"}
[**γ' — Spoilers + suboptimal mediator + empty Putnam win-set.** [IRGC = total spoiler]{.gloss data-gloss="stedman-spoilers"} (regime-survival stake from Q2 α); Netanyahu = limited spoiler (regime-change red line from Q11). [Pakistan's Kydd-bias]{.gloss data-gloss="kydd-biased-mediator"} is suboptimal *in the wrong direction* — NATO-ally + Sunni-majority + Saudi-aligned makes Iran discount Pakistani endorsements of US concessions. **Oman would have been better-configured.** Trump ∩ IRGC ∩ Netanyahu Level-II win-set = ∅.]{.concise-only}

::: {.deep-only}
**Mechanism γ' — Spoiler dynamics + Putnam win-set non-overlap + [Kydd]{.gloss data-gloss="kydd-biased-mediator"} biased-mediator misconfiguration** (P operative 0.80; P load-bearing 0.50). The framework combination: [Stedman 1997]{.gloss data-gloss="stedman-spoilers"} classifies spoilers into limited (specific limited goals; can be inducted), greedy (maximalist but expandable goals; require coercion), and total (oppose any peace agreement; require coercion or elimination) — and identifies three custodian strategies (coercion, inducement, socialization). Kydd 2003 argues biased mediators are more effective than neutral ones when their endorsements carry information that aligns with the disfavored side's beliefs. Putnam 1988 frames settlements as requiring Level-II win-set overlap. The Q3 application: *IRGC under Vahidi = total spoiler*. IRGC institutional position requires rejecting any settlement that allows external coercion of the IRGC; cannot be incentivized to compliance because regime-survival stake is existential (Q2 α-mechanism); requires coercion or elimination, neither available. *Netanyahu = limited spoiler*. Regime-change red line; can comply with limited agreements that don't preserve Iranian regime, but such an agreement violates Iran's reservation point. *Trump-faction = unclear spoiler type*. May be limited (wants visible win) or greedy (wants oil seizure + regime change); could shift to less-spoiler if domestic conditions change (Q10 falsifier 2). *Pakistan as custodian*: lacks coercion capacity (cannot militarily compel either side), lacks meaningful inducement capacity (no carrots large enough to shift either side's calculus), lacks socialization capacity (insufficient time horizon). *Pakistan's [Kydd]{.gloss data-gloss="kydd-biased-mediator"}-bias configuration is suboptimal in the wrong direction*: NATO ally + Sunni-majority + Saudi-aligned + (also) China-aligned + Muslim-majority. Mixed bias. From Iran's perspective, Pakistan reads as primarily US-NATO-Sunni biased; Iran discounts Pakistani endorsements of US concessions as not-impartial-enough. From US perspective, Pakistan reads as Muslim-Iran-sympathetic; US also discounts Pakistani endorsements of Iranian concessions. Neither side trusts Pakistani endorsements fully — *suboptimal Kydd configuration*. **Oman would have been better-configured** (perceived as Iran-trusted but quietly Western-cooperative; both sides trust Oman). The choice of Pakistan as mediator reflects power dynamics (Pakistan brokered first; Saudi-Iran rapprochement infrastructure made Pakistan acceptable to both sides at the moment of crisis), not optimal Kydd configuration. *Putnam win-set non-overlap*: Trump Level-II (producer-coalition + audience-cost-locked-in from Q10/Q2 β) ∩ IRGC Level-II (regime-survival from Q2 α) ∩ Netanyahu Level-II (regime-change red line from Q11) = ∅. No three-way overlap exists; settlement cannot pass ratification at any actor's Level-II.
:::
:::

[**The trajectory matches Beardsley + Werner-Yuen predictions point-by-point.** Three observable phases. *Phase 1 (8-18 April)*: short-term success — formal agreement achieved through Pakistan's pressure; 9-day window before first time-inconsistency manifestation. *Phase 2 (18 April → 4 May)*: accelerating violations — Iran's transit attempt, US's non-reciprocity, *Touska* seizure, dial-up to active combat by 4 May. *Phase 3 (4-8 May)*: operational collapse — Project Freedom, strikes on Iranian command nodes, multi-axis escalation. [The [Vukovic framing]{.gloss data-gloss="vukovic-nash-equilibrium"} ("Nash equilibrium nobody wants but stable") must be disambiguated: *stable AT WHAT?* **Ceasefire compliance is unstable** (Q3 finding); **war persistence is stable** (Q2 finding). Both are true simultaneously. The framing risks becoming a META rule 6 refinement rescue without disambiguation — protected from falsification by definitional flexibility. Subsumed into β' (war stable) and α' + γ' (ceasefire unstable).]{.concise-only}
[**The [Vukovic "stable Nash equilibrium" framing]{.gloss data-gloss="vukovic-nash-equilibrium"} requires disambiguation.** Vukovic 2026 argued the 2026 Iran war is converging on a Nash equilibrium that "nobody wants but is stable." Three equilibrium outcomes are possible (negotiated settlement, regime change, protracted stalemate); the third is the Nash equilibrium because the player who appears most willing to absorb mutual destruction gains leverage. The framing captures real features — both sides have lower utility under continued conflict than under their preferred alternatives; neither can achieve their preferred alternative. But the framing conflates two different stability concepts: *ceasefire compliance* and *war persistence*. The Q3 finding is that ceasefire compliance is **unstable** — the Pakistan-brokered agreement is structurally doomed by α' + β' + γ'. The Q2 finding is that war persistence is **stable** — the Iran-side regime-survival mechanism + US-side audience-cost lock-in + structural commitment-trap envelope jointly produce sustained war prosecution. Both can be true simultaneously. The Vukovic framing is correct *for war persistence*; wrong *for ceasefire compliance*. Without disambiguation, the framing risks becoming a META rule 6 refinement rescue — protected from falsification by definitional flexibility. The Q3 contribution: subsume Vukovic into the multi-framework analysis with explicit disambiguation, rather than preserving as a separate finding.]{.deep-only}

## Pre-mortem {#pre-mortem}

The most likely ways the analysis will be wrong:

1. **Beardsley time-inconsistency applied incorrectly** (P ≈ 0.15). Beardsley framework doesn't generalize from interstate-crisis-with-mediation (1918-2001 ICB sample) to active-warfare-ceasefire-with-mediation. Mitigation: Beardsley's three mechanisms (information, leverage, monitoring/enforcement) are theoretically general; should apply.

2. **Werner-Yuen H1 misapplied** (P ≈ 0.15). Iran-US battle outcomes are actually consistent (e.g., US is decisively winning per RAND assessment). Mitigation: empirical evidence supports inconsistent battles — Iran retains chokepoint denial despite massive US air campaign; this is the textbook Pape coercion-failure case.

3. **Stedman spoiler classifications wrong** (P ≈ 0.20). IRGC is greedy rather than total spoiler (would settle for limited terms that preserve some institutional position), or Netanyahu is more limited than estimated. Mitigation: classifications are tentative; framework still applies with category adjustments.

4. **Pakistan Kydd-bias is actually optimal** (P ≈ 0.15). Pakistan's mixed bias is perceived by both sides as effectively neutral. Mitigation: Iran's and Trump's revealed reservation points both diverge from Pakistan's positions; suggests Iran doesn't trust Pakistan-as-pro-Iran or US-as-pro-US fully.

5. **Vukovic stability framing is actually right** (P ≈ 0.20). Violations stabilize at low-intensity steady-state by 60-day mark; ceasefire-as-stable-equilibrium reading would be empirically supported. Mitigation: current trajectory (4 May escalation + 7-8 May further escalation) is inconsistent with stabilization; but base-rate-wise some interstate ceasefires do stabilize at low-intensity (Korean DMZ pattern).

6. **Information convergence might end the war** (P ≈ 0.20). Sustained dual blockade produces enough information convergence (Wagner/Reiter mechanism) to enable bargaining range overlap. Mitigation: 90-day horizon insufficient for information convergence; multi-year horizon possible.

**Total probability the finding is substantively wrong**: ≈ 0.30 (with overlap; not strictly additive). Consistent with the META-rule-5-capped posterior of 0.75.

## Pre-1979 historical lineage

The closest historical analog to the Pakistan-brokered 8 April 2026 ceasefire's structural instability is the **1954 IOP consortium agreement**. That agreement was technically generous — the 50/50 deal AIOC had refused Mosaddegh — but the coercive origin (the 1953 Anglo-American coup that removed Mosaddegh) made it structurally unstable for the 25 years from 1954 to 1979 nationalization. The IOP composition (BP 40%, Royal Dutch Shell 14%, five US majors 8% each, CFP 6%) defined Iran's oil-rentier structure but was always vulnerable to renunciation once the underlying power-balance shifted. The base rate Q3 reads from this case: **settlements through coercion are structurally fragile even when their terms are objectively favorable.**

The 1954 IOP case fires both Werner-Yuen H1 (battle-inconsistency before agreement — Mosaddegh's National Front retained significant base) and H2 (interrupted-war pattern — third-party pressure from the CIA-MI6 team produced the agreement). Walter 1997's third-party enforcement requirement was *partially* met (US/UK security guarantee against Soviet penetration; SAVAK as domestic enforcement), which is why the 1954 deal lasted 25 years rather than collapsing immediately. The 2026 Pakistan-brokered ceasefire lacks even that partial Walter condition (no third-party enforcer; UNSC vetoes preclude any) — predicting *much faster collapse* than the 25-year IOP precedent. The 8 April → 8 May violation cascade is consistent with the prediction.
